claims.claim: Family development is the study of how families change across the life course; the family-development research tradition, associated with Evelyn Duvall's classic mid-century work, treats the family unit itself — its membership, roles, and relationships — as what develops over time.

The family life cycle is the classic framing, associated with Evelyn Duvall, that pictures families moving through recognizable stages; an orientation-level account names four broad stages: formation, child-rearing, launching, and later life.

Family formation typically happens in early adulthood — partners set up households together and often become parents — and families remain the primary support for the young-adult transition, providing on average 10 percent of their income to their young adult children.

Parenting is the caregiving role of raising children; it is a central job of the child-rearing years and it changes shape as children grow, with parent-child relationships adjusting as children become more independent.
Launching is the process in which children transition from being dependent on their parents to being independent young adults; the experience is shaped by economic and cultural factors.

The sandwich generation consists of adults who have a parent age 65 or older and are either raising at least one child younger than 18 or providing financial support to an adult child; about 23 percent of U.S. adults fit this description, and 54 percent of Americans in their 40s do.

Midlife adults are often engaged in the care of children, aging parents, or grandchildren at the same time; caring for both children and aging relatives at once is linked with greater financial and emotional strain (caregiver burden) than caring only for aging parents, and millions of Americans provide care for a friend or family member with a serious health condition.

Family forms vary widely: 62 percent of U.S. children under 18 live with two married parents (an all-time low), 26 percent live with a single parent, and about 5 percent live with neither parent, most raised by grandparents; modern households also include multigenerational, blended, same-sex-parent, empty-nest, and skipped-generation arrangements.
Families function as living systems: interconnected units in which a change in one member ripples through the others, so that a family at any single moment is best read as a slice of a longer story.
In later life families keep developing: adult children and aging parents renegotiate roles, grandparenting begins, and caregiving can flow in both directions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How common is the sandwich generation?
positions: Pew Research Center (survey, October 2021): 23 percent of U.S. adults have a parent 65+ and are raising a child under 18 or financially supporting an adult child
OpenStax Lifespan Development 14.4 cites an AARP figure (2001): 25 percent of U.S. adults simultaneously providing unpaid care for a dependent child and an aging parent
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The two figures use different definitions (age of parent, type of support), different years, and different samples. The lesson uses Pew's current definition and figure (23 percent; 54 percent of people in their 40s) and presents the sandwich generation as a widely shared situation rather than a precise universal number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the family life cycle a universal sequence or a descriptive lens?
positions: Classic framing (Duvall): families move through a recognizable sequence of stages from formation to later life
Modern evidence: family forms and the order of transitions vary widely (single parents, grandparents raising grandchildren, blended and multigenerational households, families without children)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the classic stages as an orientation and explicitly frames them as a lens, not a script, supported by Pew family-form data and OpenStax's list of household types. No family is judged against the cycle as a standard.
